newsitem.title: GERMANY: Revaluation won't hurt Bundesbank solidity - Waigel.
newsitem.headline: Revaluation won't hurt Bundesbank solidity - Waigel.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Monday that Bonn's plan to revalue its gold and currency reserves will not undermine the solidity of the Bundesbank.
"The reorganisation of the accounts of the Bundesbank will be undertaken with the required caution," he said. "The financial solidity of the Bundesbank will be maintained.

The provision for currency risks will remain clearly recognisable for the markets, Waigel said at conference on European economic and monetary union that was organised by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democratic party.
The revaluation of the reserves was part of the harmonisation of accounting with the European central bank. "Taking over the accounting principles foreseen for the ECB is sensible," he said.
Waigel also warned against the idea of weakening the Maastricht treaty target requiring public deficits totaling no more than three percent of gross domestic product.
"I warn against such a discussion which would lead to a reaction not only in Germany," he said.
Waigel also said the decision on which countries would join EMU at the planned 1999 start would not become clear until European finance ministers meet to discuss the matter next year.
"Convergence dictates the timetable -- for every single country," Waigel said. Until the May 1998 meeting on the decision, "speculation over the group of members would be pointless."
Waigel said Bonn wanted a strict interpretation of the entry rules, even though Germany was struggling to meet the Maastricht criteria.

"For the government, a narrow and strict application of the treaty rules when examining convergence is vital. Markets and citizens expect that," he said. "Both houses of parliament and the constitutional court have demanded strict and narrow" interpretation.

He also said no countries would be given special consideration. "A chain is only as strong as its weakest link. Therefore only equally strong stability-based (countries) can join in at the start of currency union," he said.
Waigel added that it would be possible for countries to join EMU later through the revised exchange rate mechanism while pressing on with efforts to converge with the euro-countries.
"Nobody will be discriminated against or left behind, but the euro-countries will offer all the others an anchor of stability."
In order to meet the Maastricht borrowing requirement, Waigel said he would press ahead with privatisation of state property holdings and shares in Deutsche Telekom AG.
He would also maintain tight control on departmental spending, and said he did not rule out the option of a budget freeze.
